chunks: LDO efficiency vs current and dropout. The question: LDO efficiency analysis. How does output current and dropout voltage impact efficiency?
An LDO's efficiency is mostly set by the voltage ratio V out over V in , not by the load current. Two things change this.
At very light load, the chip's own quiescent current becomes a big share of what it draws.
At high current, the dropout grows, so you need more headroom, and efficiency at that headroom is lower. To get the best efficiency, keep the input close to the minimum it needs.
Think of a car engine at idle. Even with no driving, it burns some fuel, and that matters only when you are driving very little.
At a normal speed the idle fuel is a tiny part of the total. The LDO's quiescent current acts like the idle fuel.
The analogy leaves out dropout, which is more like needing a bigger road for a bigger truck: more current needs more headroom.
Three regions. Below about 1 milliamps, I Q pulls efficiency down (half of the ideal at I out equals I Q equals 50 micro A). From a few mA up to about 0.
9 amps efficiency is flat at V out over V in equals 89. 2 % .
Above 1 amps the input is below V out plus V DO : the LDO is out of regulation, the output follows V in-IR DS(on) and "efficiency" falls (87% at 1. 2 amps, 84% at 1.
5 amps), but the output voltage is also below 3. 3 volts, so the load may misbehave. Drag I Q up to 1 milliamps: the light-load drop moves up by more than a decade.
Drag V in up to 5 volts: the flat part falls to 66% and the dropout current moves off the right edge.
Efficiency: output power divided by input power ("LDO meaning and dropout advantage"). Quiescent current ( I Q ): the current the regulator uses for itself.
Headroom: the actual V in-V out in your circuit. Dropout voltage: the minimum headroom, about the load current times the pass transistor's smallest resistance ( R DS(on) ).
Light load: a load current comparable to I Q .
Take 5 volts in, 3. 3 volts out. At 0. 1 amps or at 1 amps, the efficiency is about 3. 3 over 5 equals 66 % . Now use the smallest input that works, 3.
5 volts, and the efficiency rises to about 3. 3 over 3. 5 equals 94 % .
At light load, if the load current is only one fifth of I Q , the efficiency drops to one sixth of the ideal, so 66 % becomes about 11%. That is the whole idea.
"Efficiency is V outI out over [V in(I out plus I Q)] , essentially V out over V in when the load is much bigger than I Q , so it's flat versus load current.

Output current matters at light load, where I Q dominates, and at heavy load through dropout: V DO equals I R DS(on) raises the minimum input, and at that minimum the best efficiency is V out over (V out plus V DO) .
E. g. 3. 3 volts with 200 millivolts dropout gives 94%, but headroom of 1. 7 volts gives only 66%."
